quarterly_data.signal: SHARE INSIDE BUMP-PACKAGING INSPECTION, AND HYBRID BONDING AS THE NEXT STEP: Ahmad Khan (President of Semiconductor Products and Customers) says KLA entered advanced packaging about five, six years ago with 10% share and is 'Now we are above 50%, 56%, 57% share in advanced packaging', driven by capability requirements; he notes this is still bump packaging. Hybrid bonding / die-to-wafer bonding in logic (SOIC) brings 'a 10x change in specifications of defects that kill the die', pulling KLA's most advanced front-end systems into packaging, and the introduction of hybrid bonding in memory will tighten specs significantly as well. Economics: a logic wafer out of the front-end fab is worth '$30,000, $40,000, $50,000' and a memory wafer '$50,000, $60,000, $70,000', so a loss in packaging also loses that wafer's value and customers 'want to inspect every step'.
quarterly_data.figure: 10% share about five, six years ago to 56%, 57% share; hybrid bonding a 10x change in specifications of defects that kill the die

quarterly_data.signal: TERAFAB NAMED AS A NEW CUSTOMER ENGAGEMENT: Ahmad Khan lists 'new customers coming in as you know, like Terafab and others' among U.S. fab builders. On the engagement he says Terafab is 'engaged in an R&D line first' and KLA is working with them to develop those processes, including process transfers from other customers' developed nodes; 'as Terafab starts building that initial factory, we would be engaged with them on that, and then as they go forward with HBM fab, we’ll be engaged with them.' KLA also had a prior relationship with them on other parts of their businesses that need advanced packaging and chip integration. No order size or timing was given. (Terafab was first raised by Khan himself; the moderator then asked about it.)

SUPPLY-CHAIN ACTIONS BEHIND THE CONSTRAINT: Higgins says the memory issue 'has been more of a cost issue than it’s been a supply issue' - KLA first secured supply 'to meet our needs for 2026 and 2027', then had to secure more at much higher prices (the roughly 100-ish basis points gross-margin headwind already cited). For optics and other long-lead custom parts, KLA makes investments with suppliers that show up as 'large prepaids or sharing of CapEx'. On its own capacity, in November Higgins will attend a ribbon cutting on a Singapore building he broke ground on two years ago plus a groundbreaking on the next building. He also said 'I could ship more if I had more parts even today.' Context on KLA as a compute buyer: Khan says an average high-end KLA machine takes 'about one petabyte of images per day', and KLA has moved its systems to a GPU-based compute architecture using GPUs and memory.
quarterly_data.figure: secured supply for needs for 2026 and 2027; large prepaids or sharing of CapEx; Singapore expansion groundbreaking in November; about one petabyte of images per day

quarterly_data.signal: LEGACY / CHINA SIZED FOR 2027: Higgins says in the legacy parts of the market, including China, 'you will start to see some growth again'; it is 'a smaller part of the business, maybe 25-ish percent of overall WFE', and will not grow as fast as the overall market, so its percent of the total 'maybe comes down'. He also said that from a share point of view in the expanding U.S. footprint KLA is 'at least sort of flattish'.
quarterly_data.figure: legacy including China maybe 25-ish percent of overall WFE
